nodes.text: Testing an AI agent idea on real digital tasks (fixing code, browsing the web, using tools) requires building sandboxing, tool interfaces, and evaluation harnesses before any experiment can run.
Without a shared platform, every research group re-implements this infrastructure, and results across groups are hard to compare because they use different harnesses and agents.

Prior benchmark-specific evaluations exist for individual domains: software-repair benchmarks (e.g. SWE-Bench Lite, HumanEvalFix), web-interaction benchmarks (WebArena, MiniWoB++), and general tool-use/reasoning benchmarks (GAIA, GPQA, AgentBench, MINT, ProofWriter, Entity Deduction Arena), each with its own baseline agents.

The evidence available to this paper does not include a verified comparison of OpenHands against other agent frameworks feature-by-feature (the source paper's framework-comparison table is not readable in this evidence package); what is documented is that evaluation in this space is organized as separate per-domain benchmark families rather than a single shared harness spanning them.

Can one general-purpose agent, run without per-domain modification, be evaluated end to end across software-engineering, web-interaction, and miscellaneous-assistance tasks through a single platform and harness?
Provide an open platform (agent hub + evaluation framework over 15 benchmarks) and measure one agent's behavior across the three task categories it defines.

OpenHands: an agent hub of implemented agents (a general CodeAct-style agent, a browsing agent, and others) plus an evaluation framework integrating 15 established benchmarks across software, web, and misc.-assistance categories, released under the MIT license.
Software-engineering evaluation: SWE-Bench Lite (300 instances) and HumanEvalFix (164 instances), 0-shot, no hint text, comparing CodeActAgent against tool-based and non-agentic baselines.
CodeActAgent v1.8 (claude-3-5-sonnet) resolves 26.0% of SWE-Bench Lite; CodeActAgent v1.5 (gpt-4o) fixes 79.3% of HumanEvalFix (Python).

Web-interaction evaluation: WebArena (812 instances, zero-shot) and MiniWoB++ (125 environments, full set), comparing BrowsingAgent against domain-general prompted agents and trained/reward-model specialists.

BrowsingAgent v1.0 (claude-3.5-sonnet) reaches 15.5% on WebArena, below AutoWebGLM (18.2%) and Auto Eval & Refine (20.2%); BrowsingAgent v1.0 (gpt-4o) reaches 40.8% on MiniWoB++, far below the trained specialist CC-NET (91.1%).

Miscellaneous-assistance evaluation: GAIA (53 L1-validation instances), GPQA-diamond (198 instances), AgentBench OS (144 instances), MINT math/code (225/136 instances), ProofWriter (600, 5-hop subset), and Entity Deduction Arena (200 instances).

CodeActAgent/GPTSwarm reach 32.1% on GAIA (vs. AutoGPT 13.2%), 52.0-53.1% on GPQA-diamond, 57.6% on AgentBench OS (vs. baseline 42.4%), 77.3% on MINT math (vs. baseline 65.8%), and 78.8% on ProofWriter (vs. Logic-LM 79.6%).
On MINT code, OpenHands scores 50.0% vs. baseline 59.6%; on Entity Deduction Arena, 38.0% vs. baseline 40.0%.

The same unmodified CodeAct agent performs at levels the authors describe as competitive in several categories (software repair, some misc.-assistance tasks) while trailing specialized or trained baselines in others (web interaction, MiniWoB++, MINT code, Entity Deduction Arena).

A single open platform and harness let one general agent be measured, without per-domain modification, across 15 benchmarks spanning three digital-task categories, providing a shared basis for comparing future agents.
All reported numbers are single-run point estimates with no variance, and two pairs of reported numbers conflict internally in the source material.

Because the harness and agent are open and reusable, other researchers can extend the agent hub or add benchmarks without re-building the platform, and can directly compare new agents against the reported numbers under the caveats in N17.
The authors name closing the remaining gap on HumanEvalFix (targeting 100%) and reducing handcrafted workflow engineering as future directions.

An LLM agent here means a large language model wrapped in a loop that observes an environment, chooses an action (e.g. a shell command, a browser action, a code edit), and repeats until the task is judged complete or a turn limit is reached.

experiment_chains.hypothesis: A general CodeAct agent, without task-specific tuning, can repair real repository issues and fix buggy functions at rates comparable to specialized coding agents.
experiment_chains.falsifier: The agent scores far below tool-based coding baselines (Agentless, Moatless, Aider) or non-agentic baselines (StarCoder2-15B).
experiment_chains.design_rationale: SWE-Bench Lite (300 instances, w/o hint, 0-shot) and HumanEvalFix (164 instances, 0-shot) are established repository-fix and function-fix benchmarks already used by the compared baselines, which keeps the task definitions comparable.
experiment_chains.next: Having shown the agent is comparable on code-fix tasks, the next question is whether the same agent, unmodified, also functions in an interactive web environment.

experiment_chains.hypothesis: The same agent family, adapted only with a browsing-specific agent, can complete open-ended web tasks and structured web micro-tasks at rates competitive with other domain-general prompted agents.
experiment_chains.falsifier: The agent scores far below both domain-general prompted baselines and trained specialists.
experiment_chains.design_rationale: WebArena (812 instances) tests open-ended, realistic web tasks; MiniWoB++ (125 environments) tests short, structured interactions; together they bound the web-interaction category using benchmarks the cited baselines also report on.
experiment_chains.next: Web interaction shows a wider gap to specialized systems than code repair; the next question is whether this pattern (competitive in some places, trailing in others) also holds for general tool-use and reasoning tasks.

experiment_chains.experiment: Miscellaneous-assistance evaluation (GAIA, GPQA, AgentBench OS, MINT, ProofWriter, Entity Deduction Arena)
experiment_chains.hypothesis: The same agent, without domain-specific modification, generalizes to open-ended tool-use tasks (GAIA), knowledge-intensive QA (GPQA), OS command use (AgentBench), multi-turn code/math reasoning (MINT), logical inference (ProofWriter), and interactive deduction (Entity Deduction Arena).
experiment_chains.falsifier: The agent underperforms baseline agents across most of these tasks, indicating the generalist design does not transfer beyond code and web tasks.
experiment_chains.design_rationale: These six benchmarks were selected in the evidence package as the paper's own miscellaneous-assistance category; each has a published baseline agent or reference method the paper compares against.
experiment_chains.next: Across all three categories the pattern is mixed rather than uniformly superior, which motivates the interpretation that the contribution is the shared platform and generalist evaluation, not a per-benchmark state-of-the-art result.
